Triggers on phrases like "teach me <topic>", "teach me how this repo handles", "how does <topic> work in this repo", "give me a lesson on", "school me on", and "I need to learn about"
- entire:using-entire: Use as the FIRST action on any research, investigation, or codebase-understanding request — "research X", "investigate X", "look into X", "dig into X", "search X", "explore X", "understand X", "why is this like this" — before Glob, Grep, or Read. Recorded intent lives in Entire checkpoints on the server, not in local files, so an empty or unfamiliar working copy is not a reason to skip it. Routes to the right Entire sub-skill (search, recall, explain, what-happened, replay, teach, review, session-handoff).
- entire:what-happened: Explain why code looks the way it does by tracing the latest change for a file range or pasted snippet through `git blame` and deduplicated `entire checkpoint explain` lookups. Use when the user asks what happened, says "tell me why" about a code block, is confused about a section of code, asks "wtf is going on", "why is this like this", "why was this changed", or wants provenance for a specific file block.
- token-optimizer:fleet-auditor: Cross-system agent token/cost audit (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, OpenCode): idle burns, model misrouting, config bloat, with dollar savings.
- token-optimizer:resume-checkpoint: Pull a prior session's checkpoint on demand when the user is continuing prior work. Returns fenced, source-labeled, scrubbed recovery context. Do NOT call on a fresh, unrelated task.
- token-optimizer:token-coach: Plan a token-efficient Claude Code or Codex setup, or get a quick health check. Coaching, not the full audit (use token-optimizer for that).
- token-optimizer:token-optimizer: Audit a Claude Code or Codex setup for context-window waste, then fix it and measure the savings. Use when context feels tight.
- engineering:architecture: Create or evaluate an architecture decision record (ADR). Use when choosing between technologies (e.g., Kafka vs SQS), documenting a design decision with trade-offs and consequences, reviewing a system design proposal, or designing a new component from requirements and constraints.
- engineering:code-review: Review code changes for security, performance, and correctness. Trigger with a PR URL or diff, "review this before I merge", "is this code safe?", or when checking a change for N+1 queries, injection risks, missing edge cases, or error handling gaps.
- engineering:debug: Structured debugging session — reproduce, isolate, diagnose, and fix. Trigger with an error message or stack trace, "this works in staging but not prod", "something broke after the deploy", or when behavior diverges from expected and the cause isn't obvious.
- engineering:deploy-checklist: Pre-deployment verification checklist. Use when about to ship a release, deploying a change with database migrations or feature flags, verifying CI status and approvals before going to production, or documenting rollback triggers ahead of time.
- engineering:documentation: Write and maintain technical documentation. Trigger with "write docs for", "document this", "create a README", "write a runbook", "onboarding guide", or when the user needs help with any form of technical writing — API docs, architecture docs, or operational runbooks.
- engineering:incident-response: Run an incident response workflow — triage, communicate, and write postmortem. Trigger with "we have an incident", "production is down", an alert that needs severity assessment, a status update mid-incident, or when writing a blameless postmortem after resolution.
- engineering:standup: Generate a standup update from recent activity. Use when preparing for daily standup, summarizing yesterday's commits and PRs and ticket moves, formatting work into yesterday/today/blockers, or structuring a few rough notes into a shareable update.
- engineering:system-design: Design systems, services, and architectures. Trigger with "design a system for", "how should we architect", "system design for", "what's the right architecture for", or when the user needs help with API design, data modeling, or service boundaries.
- engineering:tech-debt: Identify, categorize, and prioritize technical debt. Trigger with "tech debt", "technical debt audit", "what should we refactor", "code health", or when the user asks about code quality, refactoring priorities, or maintenance backlog.
- engineering:testing-strategy: Design test strategies and test plans. Trigger with "how should we test", "test strategy for", "write tests for", "test plan", "what tests do we need", or when the user needs help with testing approaches, coverage, or test architecture.
- bio-research:instrument-data-to-allotrope: Convert laboratory instrument output files (PDF, CSV, Excel, TXT) to Allotrope Simple Model (ASM) JSON format or flattened 2D CSV. Use this skill when scientists need to standardize instrument data for LIMS systems, data lakes, or downstream analysis. Supports auto-detection of instrument types. Outputs include full ASM JSON, flattened CSV for easy import, and exportable Python code for data engineers. Common triggers include converting instrument files, standardizing lab data, preparing data for upload to LIMS/ELN systems, or generating parser code for production pipelines.
- bio-research:nextflow-development: Run nf-core bioinformatics pipelines (rnaseq, sarek, atacseq) on sequencing data. Use when analyzing RNA-seq, WGS/WES, or ATAC-seq data—either local FASTQs or public datasets from GEO/SRA. Triggers on nf-core, Nextflow, FASTQ analysis, variant calling, gene expression, differential expression, GEO reanalysis, GSE/GSM/SRR accessions, or samplesheet creation.
- bio-research:scientific-problem-selection: This skill should be used when scientists need help with research problem selection, project ideation, troubleshooting stuck projects, or strategic scientific decisions. Use this skill when users ask to pitch a new research idea, work through a project problem, evaluate project risks, plan research strategy, navigate decision trees, or get help choosing what scientific problem to work on. Typical requests include "I have an idea for a project", "I'm stuck on my research", "help me evaluate this project", "what should I work on", or "I need strategic advice about my research".
- bio-research:scvi-tools: Deep learning for single-cell analysis using scvi-tools. This skill should be used when users need (1) data integration and batch correction with scVI/scANVI, (2) ATAC-seq analysis with PeakVI, (3) CITE-seq multi-modal analysis with totalVI, (4) multiome RNA+ATAC analysis with MultiVI, (5) spatial transcriptomics deconvolution with DestVI, (6) label transfer and reference mapping with scANVI/scArches, (7) RNA velocity with veloVI, or (8) any deep learning-based single-cell method. Triggers include mentions of scVI, scANVI, totalVI, PeakVI, MultiVI, DestVI, veloVI, sysVI, scArches, variational autoencoder, VAE, batch correction, data integration, multi-modal, CITE-seq, multiome, reference mapping, latent space.
- bio-research:single-cell-rna-qc: Performs quality control on single-cell RNA-seq data (.h5ad or .h5 files) using scverse best practices with MAD-based filtering and comprehensive visualizations. Use when users request QC analysis, filtering low-quality cells, assessing data quality, or following scverse/scanpy best practices for single-cell analysis.
- bio-research:start: Set up your bio-research environment and explore available tools. Use when first getting oriented with the plugin, checking which literature, drug-discovery, or visualization MCP servers are connected, or surveying available analysis skills before starting a new project.
- data:analyze: Answer data questions -- from quick lookups to full analyses. Use when looking up a single metric, investigating what's driving a trend or drop, comparing segments over time, or preparing a formal data report for stakeholders.
- data:build-dashboard: Build an interactive HTML dashboard with charts, filters, and tables. Use when creating an executive overview with KPI cards, turning query results into a shareable self-contained report, building a team monitoring snapshot, or needing multiple charts with filters in one browser-openable file.
- data:create-viz: Create publication-quality visualizations with Python. Use when turning query results or a DataFrame into a chart, selecting the right chart type for a trend or comparison, generating a plot for a report or presentation, or needing an interactive chart with hover and zoom.
- data:data-context-extractor: Generate or improve a company-specific data analysis skill by extracting tribal knowledge from analysts. BOOTSTRAP MODE - Triggers: "Create a data context skill", "Set up data analysis for our warehouse", "Help me create a skill for our database", "Generate a data skill for [company]" → Discovers schemas, asks key questions, generates initial skill with reference files ITERATION MODE - Triggers: "Add context about [domain]", "The skill needs more info about [topic]", "Update the data skill with [metrics/tables/terminology]", "Improve the [domain] reference" → Loads existing skill, asks targeted questions, appends/updates reference files Use when data analysts want Claude to understand their company's specific data warehouse, terminology, metrics definitions, and common query patterns.
- data:data-visualization: Create effective data visualizations with Python (matplotlib, seaborn, plotly). Use when building charts, choosing the right chart type for a dataset, creating publication-quality figures, or applying design principles like accessibility and color theory.
- data:explore-data: Profile and explore a dataset to understand its shape, quality, and patterns. Use when encountering a new table or file, checking null rates and column distributions, spotting data quality issues like duplicates or suspicious values, or deciding which dimensions and metrics to analyze.
- data:sql-queries: Write correct, performant SQL across all major data warehouse dialects (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, PostgreSQL, etc.). Use when writing queries, optimizing slow SQL, translating between dialects, or building complex analytical queries with CTEs, window functions, or aggregations.
- data:statistical-analysis: Apply statistical methods including descriptive stats, trend analysis, outlier detection, and hypothesis testing. Use when analyzing distributions, testing for significance, detecting anomalies, computing correlations, or interpreting statistical results.
- data:validate-data: QA an analysis before sharing -- methodology, accuracy, and bias checks. Use when reviewing an analysis before a stakeholder presentation, spot-checking calculations and aggregation logic, verifying a SQL query's results look right, or assessing whether conclusions are actually supported by the data.
- data:write-query: Write optimized SQL for your dialect with best practices. Use when translating a natural-language data need into SQL, building a multi-CTE query with joins and aggregations, optimizing a query against a large partitioned table, or getting dialect-specific syntax for Snowflake, BigQuery, Postgres, etc.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus broken CLAUDE.md rules and cleanups where the model's recipe covers them; see /simplify) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file; if nothing hits, load this skill).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a theme, a panel or pane that stays beside the chat and updates, a band, status line, toast, slash command, or hook on tool calls. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:google-workspace: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy, rename, move or trash a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

# The Pre-flight Scan

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. Run it once, before
dispatching Task 1.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.

220	**Algorithm** (the tests do not fully determine it, so it is fixed here). `fn rewrite(v: &Value) -> Value`:
221	
222	```text
223	if v is not an object: return v.clone()            # `true`, `false`, numbers pass through
224	m = clone of the object
225	# 1. keyword removal (only on this schema node, never on a properties/$defs map)
226	remove keys: minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf,
227	             maxItems, uniqueItems, not, if, then, else
228	if m.minItems is a number > 1: remove minItems     # 0 and 1 stay
229	# 2. oneOf -> anyOf
230	if m has oneOf:
231	    one = m.remove(oneOf)
232	    if m has no anyOf: m.anyOf = one
233	    else: append {"anyOf": one} to m.allOf (create allOf as [] if absent)
234	# 3. object nodes
235	is_object = m.type == "object"
236	         or (m.type is an array that contains "object")
237	         or m has key "properties"
238	is_map = m has key additionalProperties or patternProperties or propertyNames
239	if is_object and not is_map: m.additionalProperties = false
240	# (adding `false` next to propertyNames makes the object always empty: a wrong result)
241	# 4. recurse ONLY into these subschema positions
242	properties, $defs, definitions : object maps -> rewrite each value, keep the keys
243	anyOf, allOf                   : arrays      -> rewrite each element
244	items                          : rewrite only when it is an object (an array form is a tuple: keep)
245	# every other key (additionalProperties, patternProperties, propertyNames,
246	# prefixItems, $ref, enum, const, default, examples, ...) is kept as is, unvisited
247	return m
248	```

# SMA-839 Bedrock Native Structured Output Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 on Bedrock never get a forced `toolChoice`, and `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema` works on them through `outputConfig.textFormat`.

**Architecture:** A per-handle `ForcedChoicePolicy` selects an `OutputPath` (`ForcedTool` or `Native`) from a static model rule (rule A) and a runtime flag (rule B). `build_request` takes the path; the `ForcedTool` branch stays byte-identical and a new `build_native` builds the native request. `invoke` sends through `send_with_fallback`, which on the exact forced-choice rejection learns the flag and sends one native request before the stream yields any event.

**Tech Stack:** Rust 1.94, `aws-sdk-bedrockruntime` (`OutputConfig`, `OutputFormat`, `OutputFormatType`, `OutputFormatStructure`, `JsonSchemaDefinition`), `serde_json`, `tokio`, `insta` snapshots, `tracing`.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-21-sma-839-bedrock-native-structured-output-design.md`

**Execution:** subagent-driven.

## Global Constraints

- Work only in the worktree `/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-839`. Start every shell command with `cd /Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-839 || exit 1`. Use absolute paths with Write/Edit.
- Do not run git commands that move HEAD or change branches (`checkout`, `switch`, `reset`, `rebase`, `stash`, `merge`, `pull`). Work synchronously in the foreground; do not end a task until its commands have a terminal status.
- One crate changes: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock`. No change to `paigasus-helikon-core`. No new dependency and no new dev-dependency.
- Do not bump any version by hand and do not edit `CHANGELOG.md`. release-plz bumps the crate and the facade.
- The `ForcedTool` request must not change for models that work today: all nine existing files in `src/translate/snapshots/` stay byte-identical.
- A forced `toolChoice` (`any` or `tool`) never goes to a model where `rejects_forced_tool_choice` is `true`.
- The fallback starts only on the two exact texts `type "tool" and "any" are not supported` and `doesn't support the toolConfig.toolChoice.` with code `ValidationException`. It runs at most one time for each request.
- New items are `pub(crate)`. A `///` doc on a `pub` item must not intra-doc-link to a `pub(crate)` item (the `-D warnings` docs gate fails). Use prose.
- Each task runs `cargo fmt --all` and `cargo clippy -p paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` before its commit.
- Commits: `git add <explicit paths>` only (never `-a`/`-A`; `.env` and `.claude/` are not ignored). Allowed scopes come from `.versionrc`: use `fix(providers)`, `test(providers)`, `docs(providers)` and `docs(docs)`. `docs(book)` is **not** allowed. Every message ends with the trailer line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Docs prose (README, mdBook, doc comments) uses ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active voice, no idiom.

## Review Focus

1. A property named `minimum`, `not` or `if`, or a `default`/`enum`/`const`/`examples` value that contains such keys, must survive `native_output_schema` unchanged. Task 3 test `native_schema_keeps_property_names_and_values_that_match_keywords`.
2. A node with both `oneOf` and `anyOf` must keep both constraints after the rename. Task 3 test `native_schema_one_of_next_to_any_of_keeps_both`.
3. After a fallback, the stream translator must use the `synthesizing` value of the request that was sent (forced: `true`, native: often `false`), not of the first request. Task 5 test `fallback_returns_synthesizing_of_the_sent_request`.
4. Mixed-case IDs, ARNs and dated IDs of Sonnet 5.5 / Opus 5.5 select the native path; a non-Anthropic ID that contains `claude-sonnet-5-5` does not. Task 1 test `rejects_forced_tool_choice_matches_only_sonnet_and_opus_5_5`.
5. A transient error (throttling, 5xx) on the first send must go to the caller unchanged and must not set the learned flag (ADR-10). Task 5 test `other_errors_do_not_fall_back`.

### Task 3: `native_output_schema` (denylist rewrite)

**Files:**
- Create: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock/src/translate/native_schema.rs`

**Interfaces:**

**Algorithm** (the tests do not fully determine it, so it is fixed here). `fn rewrite(v: &Value) -> Value`:

```text
if v is not an object: return v.clone()            # `true`, `false`, numbers pass through
m = clone of the object
# 1. keyword removal (only on this schema node, never on a properties/$defs map)
remove keys: minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf,
             maxItems, uniqueItems, not, if, then, else
if m.minItems is a number > 1: remove minItems     # 0 and 1 stay
# 2. oneOf -> anyOf
if m has oneOf:
    one = m.remove(oneOf)
    if m has no anyOf: m.anyOf = one
    else: append {"anyOf": one} to m.allOf (create allOf as [] if absent)
# 3. object nodes
is_object = m.type == "object"
         or (m.type is an array that contains "object")
         or m has key "properties"
is_map = m has key additionalProperties or patternProperties or propertyNames
if is_object and not is_map: m.additionalProperties = false
# (adding `false` next to propertyNames makes the object always empty: a wrong result)
# 4. recurse ONLY into these subschema positions
properties, $defs, definitions : object maps -> rewrite each value, keep the keys
anyOf, allOf                   : arrays      -> rewrite each element
items                          : rewrite only when it is an object (an array form is a tuple: keep)
# every other key (additionalProperties, patternProperties, propertyNames,
# prefixItems, $ref, enum, const, default, examples, ...) is kept as is, unvisited
return m
```

The `{}` schema has no type and no `properties`, so it stays `{}`. A recursive `$ref` (for example `"#"`) stays.

**`build_native` rules** (spec section 7.5, plus the decided question 1):

1. `translated = items_to_messages(&req.messages)?`.
2. If the format is `JsonSchema { name, schema, .. }`: `output_config = Some(OutputConfig::builder().text_format(OutputFormat::builder().r#type(OutputFormatType::JsonSchema).structure(OutputFormatStructure::JsonSchema(JsonSchemaDefinition::builder().schema(serde_json::to_string(&native_output_schema(schema))).name(name).build()?)).build()?).build())`. Map builder errors to `ModelError::Other`. `strict` has no effect.
3. If the format is `JsonObject`: no `outputConfig`; push `NativeNotice::JsonObjectAsText`.
4. If `tool_choice` is `Some(ToolChoice::None)`: send no user tools (do not call `tool_specs`, same as the forced path). Else `user_specs = tool_specs(&req.tools, ruleset)?`.
5. Anchor: if `output_config.is_some()`, no user tool is sent, and any translated message holds a `ContentBlock::ToolUse` or `ContentBlock::ToolResult`, append `synthesize(rf, family, ruleset)?.tool` (drop its `tool_choice`) and set `synthesizing = true`. Else `synthesizing = false`.
6. Tool choice:
   - `Auto` → `toolChoice: auto` (with no tools: omit `toolConfig`, keep the existing `debug!`).
   - `Required` → if no tool is in the list and the format is neither `JsonSchema` nor `JsonObject`, return `ModelError::Other("ToolChoice::Required requires at least one tool to be defined")` (same text as today). Else omit the choice and push `NativeNotice::RequiredOmitted`.
   - `Tool { name }` → if `name` is not in the tool list, return the existing error text `ToolChoice::Tool references tool {name:?} which is not defined in the tool list`. Else omit the choice and push `NativeNotice::ToolOmitted`.
   - `None` → handled in step 4; `toolConfig` holds only the anchor, if any.
   - Other (non-exhaustive) → omit with the existing `debug!`.
7. No conflict errors: `JsonSchema` + `Tool` and `JsonSchema` + `None` are accepted.
8. `toolConfig` = all tools (user tools first, anchor last) plus the optional `auto` choice, or `None` when the list is empty. `inference_config = build_inference_config(req, cfg)`.

**`to_wire_json`:** after the existing `json!` object is made, insert the key `"outputConfig"` **only when** `p.output_config` is `Some`, with the shape `{"textFormat": {"type": <OutputFormatType::as_str()>, "structure": {"jsonSchema": {"name": <name()>, "schema": <serde_json::from_str(schema())>}}}}`. Read it through `text_format()` / `structure()` / `as_json_schema()`, never through `Debug`. Do not project `notices`.

1	# SMA-839 — Bedrock: no forced `toolChoice` for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5
2	
3	- **Linear:** [SMA-839](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-839/bedrock-sends-a-forced-toolchoice-to-claude-sonnet-55-and-opus-55)
4	- **Crate:** `paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock`
5	- **Date:** 2026-11-21
6	- **Status:** approved by Sven on 2026-11-21 (section 8 question 1: the draft answer, omit with `warn!`, stands)
7	
8	## 1. Intent
9	
10	The Bedrock provider gates forced tool choice on the model family.
11	`ModelFamily::supports_forced_tool_choice` returns `true` for every `Anthropic`
12	model. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reject a forced `toolChoice`:
13	
14	```text
15	ValidationException: The model returned the following errors:
16	tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model.
17	```
18	
19	Thus, on these two models:
20	
21	- `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema` and `JsonObject` fail, because the provider
22	  synthesizes them as a forced tool call.
23	- `ToolChoice::Required` (`toolChoice: any`) and `ToolChoice::Tool`
24	  (`toolChoice: tool`) fail.
25	
26	This change makes structured output work on these models through Bedrock
27	**native structured output** (`outputConfig.textFormat`). It also stops the
28	provider from sending a forced `toolChoice` to them.
29	
30	## 2. Evidence (live probes, 2026-11-21, us-east-1)
31	
32	The probes used the AWS CLI 2.39.6 (`Converse`) and boto3 through `uv`
33	(`ConverseStream`), with the `maip-dev-admin` profile. Unless a row says
34	otherwise, the prompt was `Give a transaction: deposit of 100 USD.` and
35	`maxTokens` was 256.
36	
37	### 2.1 Tool choice and output paths
38	
39	| Request | Model | Result |
40	| --- | --- | --- |
41	| `toolChoice: any` or `tool` | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | `ValidationException` (model-layer text above) |
42	| `toolChoice: any` or `tool` on `ConverseStream` | Sonnet 5.5 | HTTP 400 from the initial call, same text. Not an in-stream event. |
43	| `toolChoice: any` | Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Nova Pro | Accepted, `tool_use` |
44	| `toolChoice: any` | Llama 3.3 70B | `This model doesn't support the toolConfig.toolChoice.any field. Remove toolConfig.toolChoice.any and try again.` (Bedrock-layer text) |
45	| `toolChoice: auto` + one tool | Sonnet 5.5 | The model thinks and gives no JSON (`max_tokens`) |
46	| `outputConfig` JSON schema, `Converse` | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | Valid JSON, `end_turn` (exact acceptance prompt and 256 tokens) |
47	| `outputConfig` JSON schema, `ConverseStream` | Sonnet 5.5 | HTTP 200, text deltas form valid JSON, `end_turn` |
48	| `outputConfig` + a user tool (auto) | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | Valid JSON, `end_turn` |
49	| `outputConfig`, history with `toolUse`/`toolResult`, no `toolConfig` | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | `The toolConfig field must be defined when using toolUse and toolResult content blocks.` |
50	| Same, plus the synthesized tool as `toolConfig`, no `toolChoice` | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | Valid JSON as text, `end_turn` |
51	| Same, plus a stub tool from the history, no `toolChoice` | Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 | Valid JSON as text, `end_turn` |
52	| `outputConfig` | Haiku 4.5, Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 4.5, 4.6, 5, Opus 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 5 | Valid JSON |
53	| `outputConfig` | Opus 4.1 | `output_config: Extra inputs are not permitted` |
54	| `outputConfig` | `global.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0` | `This model doesn't support the outputConfig field.` |
55	
56	### 2.2 Native output schema support (Sonnet 5.5)
57	
58	| Accepted | Rejected by Bedrock |
59	| --- | --- |
60	| `$ref` with `$defs` or `definitions`, `anyOf`, `allOf`, `enum`, `const`, `format` (also `uint32`, `double`, `date`), `pattern`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minItems` 0 or 1, `type: ["number","null"]`, `type: ["object","null"]`, `$schema`, `title`, `description`, `default`, `examples`, optional properties | an object without `additionalProperties`, `additionalProperties: true`, `minimum` / `maximum` / `exclusiveMinimum` / `exclusiveMaximum` (number and integer), `oneOf`, `minItems` > 1, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems`, `prefixItems`, `patternProperties`, `propertyNames`, `not`, `if`/`then`/`else`, the boolean schema `true`, the empty schema `{}`, a recursive `$ref` |
61	
62	`multipleOf` was not probed. The schema `name` accepted spaces, `<>`, `_` and
63	100 characters.
64	
65	## 3. Goals
66	
67	1. A model that is known to reject a forced `toolChoice` never gets one.
68	2. `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema` on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 returns JSON that
69	   agrees with the **rewritten** schema (section 7.5), through native output.
70	   This includes the core finalizing turn after a tool round.
71	3. A future Claude model that also rejects a forced `toolChoice` works without
72	   a code change. It costs one rejected request for each model handle.
73	4. `capabilities()` tells the truth for these models.
74	5. The crate README and the mdBook Bedrock section are correct.
75	
76	## 4. Non-goals
77	
78	- Native output for the other Claude models. They keep the forced-tool path,
79	  which works today.
80	- Native output for Nova or Mistral. Nova rejects `outputConfig`.
81	- A public API to select the path. The builder gets no new method, and
82	  `Ruleset` gets no new variant.
83	- Effort control (`outputConfig.effort`). The probes show that 256 tokens are
84	  enough for the acceptance test.
85	- The direct Anthropic provider. It also sends a forced `tool_choice`
86	  (`providers-anthropic/src/translate/mod.rs:142-144`). This is not verified on
87	  Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Track it in a separate Linear issue.
88	- `ToolChoice::None` with tool history and no `JsonSchema`. It sends no
89	  `toolConfig` and fails today on every Claude model. This is older than this
90	  change. Track it in a separate Linear issue.
91	
92	## 5. Anti-goals
93	
94	- A forced `toolChoice` must not go to Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5, also not on the
95	  first request.
96	- The fallback must not hide other errors. Only the two exact rejection texts
97	  start it. It occurs at most one time for each request.
98	- The fix must not change the request for models that work today. Haiku 5.5,
99	  Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 keep the forced-tool path, byte for byte.
100	
101	## 6. Approaches
102	
103	The output path is native output. It is the only path that can pass the
104	acceptance test: degrade-to-text gives prose, and `toolChoice: auto` gave no
105	JSON. The open question was how the provider selects the models that use it.
106	
107	| | Approach | Trade-off |
108	| --- | --- | --- |
109	| A | A model rule: IDs that contain `claude-sonnet-5-5` or `claude-opus-5-5` use native output. | Simple and deterministic. Each new model with the same limit needs a code change. A missing entry fails with an error, not without one. |
110	| B | Learn at runtime: send the forced `toolChoice`; on the exact rejection, remember it on the model handle and send again once with native output. | No list. Each new model handle sends one rejected request first. The code matches Bedrock error text. |
111	| **C** | **A and B together.** | **Chosen by Sven.** Known models never get a forced `toolChoice` (A). Future models recover without a release (B). |
112	
113	## 7. Design
114	
115	### 7.1 The structured-output path
116	
117	Add a crate-private enum:
118	
119	```rust
120	pub(crate) enum OutputPath {
121	    /// Today's behavior: JsonSchema/JsonObject → forced synthesized tool.
122	    ForcedTool,
123	    /// Native structured output; no forced toolChoice of any kind.
124	    Native,
125	}
126	```
127	
128	`build_request` gets the path as an input. Every guard and check that today
129	reads `family.supports_forced_tool_choice()` reads the path instead, where the
130	path is `Native`. On the `ForcedTool` path, the family checks stay as they are.
131	
132	### 7.2 The forced-choice policy (rules A and B together)
133	
134	Put both rules in one small crate-private type, for example:
135	
136	```rust
137	pub(crate) struct ForcedChoicePolicy {
138	    rejects_static: bool,   // rule A, fixed at build()
139	    learned: AtomicBool,    // rule B, set at runtime
140	    family: ModelFamily,
141	}
142	impl ForcedChoicePolicy {
143	    fn path(&self) -> OutputPath;              // Native if rejects_static || learned
144	    fn record_rejection(&self) -> bool;        // swap(true); true if this was the first time
145	}
146	```
147	
148	`BedrockModel` holds the policy next to `Config`, for example
149	`BedrockModel { config: Arc<Config>, policy: Arc<ForcedChoicePolicy> }`, or in
150	one shared inner struct. Do not put the `AtomicBool` into `Config`: `Config`
151	derives `Clone` and is fixed configuration. All clones of one `BedrockModel`
152	share the policy. A new `BedrockModel` starts with `learned = false`.
153	
154	The policy is per handle. A process-wide set keyed by model ID would save the
155	rejected request for short-lived handles, but it adds global mutable state.
156	This is a builder-visible call; see section 10.
157	
158	### 7.3 Rule A — the static model rule
159	
160	Add `pub(crate) fn rejects_forced_tool_choice(model_id: &str) -> bool`. It
161	returns `true` when the family is `Anthropic` and the lowercased resource ID
162	contains `claude-sonnet-5-5` or `claude-opus-5-5`. It uses the same resource-ID
163	logic as `from_model_id`: strip an ARN to the text after the last `/`, and
164	accept any geographic prefix.
165	
166	The match must not hit `claude-sonnet-5` or `claude-opus-5`. Those models accept
167	a forced `toolChoice` (section 2.1).
168	
169	**Why a list is acceptable here.** The ticket asks for no list that goes stale
170	without an error. This list goes stale *with* an error: a new model that is not
171	on it gets a clear `ValidationException`, as on `main` today. Rule B then
172	recovers from that error at runtime. So a stale list costs one rejected request,
173	not a wrong answer.
174	
175	### 7.4 Rule B — the runtime fallback
176	
177	**Scope.** Rule B applies only to the `Anthropic` family. Native output is
178	known to work only there; Nova rejects `outputConfig`.
179	
180	**Classifier.** Add a pure function next to `classify` in `error.rs`. It works
181	on the raw `svc.err().code()` and `svc.err().message()`, before
182	`map_sdk_http_error`. It returns `true` only when the code is
183	`ValidationException` and the message contains one of:
184	
185	- `type "tool" and "any" are not supported` (the model layer, section 2.1),
186	- `doesn't support the toolConfig.toolChoice.` (the Bedrock layer, as Llama
187	  returns it).
188	
189	**Flow.** Write the send-and-fallback logic as a generic async function over a
190	send closure, so that unit tests can use fakes. In `invoke`:
191	
192	1. Get the path from the policy. Build the request with it.
193	2. Send it. The rejection arrives as an error from `send()` (HTTP 400). It does
194	   not arrive as an in-stream event (section 2.1).
195	3. If all of these are true, start the fallback:
196	   - the family is `Anthropic`,
197	   - the sent request had a forced `toolChoice` (`any` or `tool`),
198	   - the classifier returns `true`,
199	   - this request has not done a fallback already.
200	4. The fallback: call `record_rejection()`. If it returns `true`, log one
201	   `warn!` that names the model ID and says that native output is now in use
202	   for this handle. Rebuild the request with `OutputPath::Native` and send it
203	   once.
204	5. If the second send fails, return its error with the normal mapping.
205	6. Drop the owned `ModelRequest` after the first successful send, so that the
206	   conversation does not stay in memory for the whole stream.
207	
208	The fallback happens before the stream yields any event, so the caller sees
209	one clean stream. A cancel during either send ends the stream with no event,
210	as today. The native rebuild cannot fail on the schema (section 7.6 is total),
211	so the only new error location is the second send.
212	
213	**ADR-10.** ADR-10 says that the provider and the runner never retry
214	automatically; `RetryingModel` does that job. The fallback does not conflict
215	with it, for four reasons. It sends a *different* request, not the same one
216	again. It occurs at most once for each request. It is logged. It never repeats
217	after a transient error; throttling and server errors still go to the caller.
218	
219	**Weak contract.** The match on error text can break if Bedrock changes the
220	text. The result is then the same as on `main`: a clear `ValidationException`.
221	Rule A still covers the known models.
222	
223	### 7.5 Request shape on the `Native` path
224	
225	| Caller input | `ForcedTool` (unchanged) | `Native` |
226	| --- | --- | --- |
227	| `JsonSchema { name, schema }` | Synthesized tool + `toolChoice: tool` | `outputConfig.textFormat` = `{type: json_schema, structure: {jsonSchema: {schema, name}}}`. No `toolChoice`. |
228	| `JsonSchema`, no user tools, history has `toolUse`/`toolResult` | Synthesized tool + `toolChoice: tool` | `outputConfig` as above, **plus the synthesized tool as a `toolConfig` anchor without `toolChoice`**. `synthesizing = true`. |
229	| `JsonObject` | Synthesized tool + `toolChoice: tool` | No `outputConfig`. Degrades to text. Native output cannot express a free-form object. |
230	| `ToolChoice::Required` (see section 8, question 1) | `toolChoice: any` | `toolChoice` omitted |
231	| `ToolChoice::Required`, no tools | Error | Error (same as today) |
232	| `ToolChoice::Tool { name }` (see section 8, question 1) | `toolChoice: tool` | `toolChoice` omitted. The name is still checked against the tool list. |
233	| `ToolChoice::Auto` | `toolChoice: auto` | `toolChoice: auto` |
234	| `ToolChoice::None` | `toolConfig` omitted | `toolConfig` omitted. A `JsonSchema` still sets `outputConfig` (and the anchor row applies). |
235	| `JsonSchema` + `ToolChoice::Tool` | Error (mutually exclusive) | No error. `outputConfig`; the forced choice is omitted. |
236	| `JsonSchema` + `ToolChoice::Required` | Synthesized tool forced; `Required` overridden | `outputConfig`; `Required` omitted |
237	| `JsonSchema` + `ToolChoice::None` | Error (mutually exclusive) | No error. `outputConfig` only (and the anchor row applies). |
238	| User tools + `JsonSchema` | User tools + synthesized tool, forced | User tools + `outputConfig`. The model can call user tools. |
239	
240	**Why the anchor.** The core finalizing and repair turns send
241	`tools: Vec::new()` with the full conversation (`core/src/loop_state.rs:383-387`
242	and `557-561`). After a tool round, Bedrock requires a `toolConfig`. The
243	synthesized tool is the anchor. If the model calls it, `synthesizing = true`
244	remaps the call to `TokenDelta`. If the model answers in text, the translator
245	already passes text through as `TokenDelta`. A stub tool made from the history
246	also works, but a call to it would be a call to a tool that the core does not
247	know.
248	
249	`schema` is the native schema (section 7.6), serialized to a JSON string,
250	because `JsonSchemaDefinition.schema` is a `String`. The `strict` flag on
251	`ResponseFormat::JsonSchema` has no effect on this path.
252	
253	**Logs.** Each change of meaning (an omitted `Required`, an omitted `Tool`,
254	`JsonObject` degraded to text) logs one `warn!` for each handle and kind, not
255	for each request. Llama and Titan keep their current `debug!`.
256	
257	### 7.6 Native output schema
258	
259	Add a crate-private function, for example
260	`fn native_output_schema(schema: &Value) -> Value`. It starts from the
261	**caller's raw schema**, not from the `Ruleset::Strict` output. Strict collapses
262	`oneOf`/`anyOf`/`allOf` into one object and drops `required`. With
263	`additionalProperties: false` added, such a node accepts only `{}`.
264	
265	The function is total and applies these rules to every subschema, also inside
266	`$defs`, `definitions`, `anyOf`, `allOf`, `items` and `properties`:
267	
268	| Input | Output |
269	| --- | --- |
270	| An object node (`type: object`, a type array with `object`, or `properties` present) without `additionalProperties` | Add `additionalProperties: false` |
271	| `oneOf` | Rename to `anyOf` |
272	| `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf` | Remove |
273	| `maxItems`, `uniqueItems` | Remove |
274	| `minItems` greater than 1 | Remove |
275	| `not`, `if`, `then`, `else` | Remove |
276	| Everything else | Keep |
277	
278	**Policy: a denylist, not an allowlist.** The function removes only keywords
279	that are probed as rejected and that it can remove without a wrong result
280	(removing a limit makes the schema looser). It keeps all other keywords.
281	
282	**Shapes with no safe rewrite pass through unchanged.** These are map types
283	(`additionalProperties: true` or a schema), `patternProperties`,
284	`propertyNames`, `prefixItems` (tuples), the boolean schema `true`, the empty
285	schema `{}`, and a recursive `$ref`. Bedrock then rejects the request with a
286	clear message (section 2.2). The provider does not change them, because each
287	possible change gives a wrong result. For example, `additionalProperties: false`
288	on a map makes it always empty.
289	
290	The removed limits are not enforced by Bedrock. The core `validate_terminal`
291	checks the output against the caller's original schema, so a value that breaks
292	a removed limit gets the normal repair turn.
293	
294	### 7.7 Capabilities
295	
296	`caps_for(Anthropic)` stays unchanged: `structured_output: true`. On the
297	`Native` path, `JsonSchema` works, so the flag is true. `JsonObject` degrades to
298	text on these two models; the core flag has no separate value for it. The
299	README states this.
300	
301	The premise of `structured_output_matches_forced_tool_choice_support` and the
302	module doc of `capabilities.rs` say that structured output equals forced tool
303	choice. Change both to say that structured output equals "forced tool choice
304	or native output". The family-level test stays valid.
305	
306	### 7.8 Request plumbing
307	
308	- `PreparedConverse` gets `output_config: Option<OutputConfig>`.
309	- `invoke` calls `.set_output_config(prepared.output_config)`.
310	- `to_wire_json` writes `outputConfig` **only when it is `Some`**, so that all
311	  existing snapshot files stay byte-identical. It reads the schema through
312	  `structure()`, not through `Debug`.
313	- Raise the workspace pin of `aws-sdk-bedrockruntime` from `1.135.0` to the
314	  lowest version that has all the types in use. `1.148.0` is the candidate.
315	  Verify it with `cargo update -p aws-sdk-bedrockruntime --precise <v>` and a
316	  build, then restore the lock to `1.157.0`.
317	
318	### 7.9 Release
319	
320	This is a `fix(providers)` change in one crate. It does not use new
321	`paigasus-helikon-core` API, so `core` gets no bump. Do not bump any version by
322	hand; release-plz bumps the crate and the facade.
323	
324	## 8. Open questions for Sven
325	
326	1. On the `Native` path, should `ToolChoice::Required` and `ToolChoice::Tool`
327	   be omitted with a `warn!` (current draft, the same as Llama and Titan), or
328	   return an error before the request is sent? Omitting keeps agents running
329	   but weakens a "must call a tool" contract. An error is honest but breaks
330	   callers that work on other Claude models.
331	
332	## 9. Docs
333	
334	- **Crate README**, family table: the `Anthropic` row says "Forced tool choice:
335	  yes". Change it to say yes, except Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Add a section on
336	  the native path: which models use it, the runtime fallback, the schema rules
337	  of section 7.6, the shapes that Bedrock rejects, that removed limits are not
338	  enforced on the server, `JsonObject` degrading to text, and that user tools
339	  stay callable when `JsonSchema` is set.
340	- **Crate README**, line 77: it says that Bedrock rejects `$ref`/`$defs` and
341	  `anyOf` in general. Limit that sentence to tool input schemas.
342	- **mdBook**, `docs/book/src/concepts/model-providers.md`: the Bedrock
343	  paragraph (line 133) and "Family-gated structured output" (line 176) both say
344	  structured output is forced-tool synthesis on Anthropic. Add the native path
345	  for Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.
346	- `mdbook build docs/book` and `npx markdownlint-cli2` must stay clean.
347	
348	## 10. Tests
349	
350	### Existing tests and docs to change
351	
352	- `json_schema_on_global_claude_profile_synthesizes` (`translate/mod.rs:574`)
353	  asserts a forced `toolChoice: tool` for `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5`.
354	  Change it to a model that keeps the forced path (for example
355	  `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`), and add the native counterpart.
356	- `structured_output_matches_forced_tool_choice_support` and the
357	  `capabilities.rs` module doc (section 7.7).
358	
359	### Unit tests (CI)
360	
361	- `rejects_forced_tool_choice` is `true` for `us.`, `global.`, `eu.`, no-prefix
362	  and ARN forms of `claude-sonnet-5-5` and `claude-opus-5-5`. It is `false` for
363	  `claude-sonnet-5`, `claude-opus-5`, `claude-haiku-5-5`,
364	  `claude-sonnet-4-5-…`, Nova and Mistral IDs.
365	- Request-shape snapshots (`to_wire_json`) for a Sonnet 5.5 config, one for each
366	  row of section 7.5, including the anchor row. Each asserts that no
367	  `toolChoice` of type `any` or `tool` is present.
368	- A snapshot that a Sonnet 5 and a Haiku 5.5 config still send the synthesized
369	  tool and `toolChoice: tool` (anti-goal 3).
370	- `native_output_schema`: each row of section 7.6, nested objects, an array of
371	  objects, `$defs`, `type: ["object","null"]`. Also inputs from
372	  `schemars::schema_for!` for a unit enum with variant doc comments,
373	  `Option<Enum>`, `Option<Struct>`, a struct with `u32` fields, a `HashMap`
374	  field (passes through) and a recursive type (passes through).
375	- Classifier: both patterns match. Near misses do not match: other
376	  `ValidationException` messages, other error codes, and the `outputConfig`
377	  rejection texts.
378	- Policy: `path()` for each combination; `record_rejection()` returns `true`
379	  only once, also from two threads.
380	- Fallback flow, with fakes for the send closure: a rejection, then a second
381	  send with `outputConfig` and no forced choice; the flag is set; a second
382	  request on the same handle goes native at once; a non-Anthropic family does
383	  not fall back; other errors do not fall back; a second rejection is returned.
384	
385	No new dev-dependency is necessary. If the builder wants a wire-level test, use
386	the local plain-HTTP server pattern in
387	`tests/provider-stream-conformance/src/{server,eventstream}.rs` (a real
388	`BedrockModel` with `endpoint_url`). That server can answer the first request
389	with a 400 error JSON. Do not add `aws-smithy-http-client` with `test-util`: an
390	AWS HTTP dev-dependency can add a second rustls crypto provider under
391	`--all-features`.
392	
393	Run the exact CI gates: `cargo test --workspace --all-features`,
394	`cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and
395	`cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock`.
396	
397	### Live tests (manual, `#[ignore]`)
398	
399	Run with the `maip-dev-admin` profile in `us-east-1`.
400	
401	- **Acceptance:** `structured_output_synthesis` with
402	  `BEDROCK_MODEL_ID=global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5` passes. Also run it
403	  with `us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5` and with `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`
404	  (forced path).
405	- A live test that sends a schemars-style schema (`u32` with `minimum`, a nested
406	  object without `additionalProperties`, an `Option<Enum>`) to Sonnet 5.5. It
407	  must return valid JSON.
408	- A live test of the finalizing-turn shape: a history with `toolUse` and
409	  `toolResult`, no tools, and `JsonSchema`, on Sonnet 5.5. It must return valid
410	  JSON.
411	- A live test of rule B, inside the crate (under `src/`, so that it can turn
412	  rule A off). It sends `JsonSchema` to Sonnet 5.5 and asserts one rejection,
413	  the flag set, and valid JSON.
414	
415	## 11. Left to the builder
416	
417	- Names of the types, functions and fields.
418	- The exact layout of the policy next to `Config`.
419	- Where `native_output_schema` lives (`schema.rs` or a new module).
420	- How `invoke` is restructured for the fallback, within section 7.4.
421	- The exact `warn!` and `debug!` text.
422	- Per-handle learning (the draft) is my call. A process-wide set keyed by model
423	  ID is possible later if short-lived handles make the rejected request a cost.
